NP-completeness of aggregate root-dependent spanning-tree cost

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript and declared publication date 6 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Original abstract

An undirected spanning tree induces an arborescence at every vertex root. Given an independent arc-cost vector for each root, we prove that deciding whether the sum of the costs of these entire rooted orientations is at most a given threshold is NP-complete, even when every cost belongs to {0,1,2}. A reduction from satisfiability uses two hubs, variable vertices, and clause vertices. A symmetric cost vector at one hub forces a tree at threshold to encode an assignment with one selected literal per clause; the corresponding clause-root costs test those literals. Uniformly shifting the costs yields the same conclusion for costs in {1,2,3}. This resolves Problem 1 in Volker Kaibel's November 2018 Oberwolfach workshop contribution, whose report was published in December 2019. Exact finite checks accompany the all-size proof.

The idea in plain English

Choosing one network tree can become computationally hard when its cost depends on the starting vertex. This note proves strong NP-completeness for the total cost of all rooted orientations, even with costs drawn from three small integers.

The precise result

Start with a finite connected simple undirected graph with N≥1 vertices. Choose one spanning tree and orient every edge away from a chosen vertex. Do this for every vertex root, keeping the same underlying tree throughout. Each root has its own independently supplied cost for every directed edge, and the objective adds the costs of all edges in all these rooted orientations.

The input explicitly lists all 2N|E| nonnegative integer costs in binary, together with an integer threshold. The decision problem asks whether some common tree has aggregate cost at most that threshold. The theorem proves strong NP-completeness already when every cost is in {0,1,2}. Finding a minimum-cost tree is therefore NP-hard. Adding one to every cost gives strong NP-completeness for the positive alphabet {1,2,3}, because every tree acquires the same total increment N(N−1).

Orienting toward each root gives an equivalent convention when every input arc-cost pair is transposed. The model charges the entire rooted tree at every root; it does not optimize a different tree for each root or charge only a selected destination path.

Why the result holds

The reduction starts from satisfiability with at most three literals per clause. Two hub vertices represent the two truth values. Variable vertices attach to hubs, and clause vertices select literals. A symmetric cost table at one hub forces every tree meeting the threshold to contain the hub edge, give each variable exactly one hub attachment, and make every clause vertex a leaf.

The forcing step accounts for every possible spanning tree. If p counts hub–variable edges, q counts clause–variable edges, and h records the hub edge, then the base cost is p+2q=K+(1−h)+(q−m), with K=2m+n and q≥m. Nonnegative costs at the other roots force h=1 and q=m at the threshold. Only after this step is the tree interpreted as an assignment.

When the tree is rooted at a clause leaf, its selected variable's edge points toward that variable's chosen hub. The clause-root table charges one precisely when this selected literal is false. Thus a satisfying assignment supplies a tree at the threshold, and a tree at the threshold supplies a satisfying assignment. The graph, every entry of the cost table, and the threshold have polynomial size. The proof handles clause simplification, empty instances, and sparse variable labels explicitly.

Scope and limitations

The result answers the whole-orientation objective in Problem 1 of Volker Kaibel's November 2018 Oberwolfach contribution, published in the workshop report in December 2019. The satisfiability machinery is classical, as developed by Cook and Karp. Martin's spanning-tree formulation is also prior work; the note credits the expositions by Conforti, Cornuéjols and Zambelli and by Friesen. Integrality of a formulation's edge projection alone does not settle arbitrary objectives on all its root-orientation variables.

The statement concerns the written finite, explicitly encoded integer-input model. It does not settle Kaibel's neighboring Problem 2 or claim NP membership for arbitrary unencoded real inputs. The false-selected-literal identity applies to the forced structured trees; it is not a formula for the unrestricted optimum in terms of the smallest number of unsatisfied clauses. Historical first discovery and present worldwide open status are not established.

The complete support archive contains the source and exact finite verification material. These checks illustrate and test the construction; the all-size reduction is what proves hardness.

sections.heading: Original abstract
paragraphs: For every fixed compact convex body K⊂ℝⁿ with nonempty interior and every real polynomial f, the normalized Lebesgue sum-of-squares density bound of degree at most 2r has error O_{K,f}(r⁻²) for every integer r≥1. We give a self-contained proof and an explicit constant, using one global square. A quadratic Taylor upper estimator reduces the objective to a scalar endpoint problem. Homothetic contraction compares every sublevel shell with the same core mass that normalizes a fixed power of a Dirichlet polynomial; that mass cancels before summation. This proves the quadratic upper rate in the convex-body/Lebesgue regime of the 2018 Oberwolfach question. A classical interval example shows that the exponent is sharp in the worst case. The proxy and the broad localization and relative-mass mechanisms have established precedents; no firstness or new-method claim is made.

sections.heading: The idea in plain English
paragraphs: A polynomial can be minimized by concentrating a sum-of-squares probability density near one of its minimizers. This note proves a quadratic error rate on every fixed full-dimensional compact convex body with Lebesgue measure, using a single global square.

sections.heading: The precise result
paragraphs: Let K⊂ℝⁿ be compact and convex with nonempty interior, with n≥1, and let f be a real polynomial. The bound Hᵣ(f,K) minimizes ∫_K f q dx over global sums of squares q of degree at most 2r subject to ∫_K q dx=1. For every integer r≥1, the error satisfies 0≤Hᵣ(f,K)−f*≤CₙG/r², where f*=min_K f.

For any minimizer a, set H=max_K ‖∇²f‖_op, γ=1+H/2, g(x)=∇f(a)·(x−a)+γ‖x−a‖², and G=max_K g. The theorem gives 0<G<∞ and the explicit constant Cₙ=4(n+2)²(π/2)^(2n+4)(1+2^(n+2)). A single square of a real polynomial, normalized over the whole body, witnesses this upper bound.

The objective need not be convex, and the boundary of K need not be smooth or semialgebraic. The same proof applies to objectives of class C² on an open neighborhood of K. The constants belong to the fixed body and objective; no useful bound uniform over all dimensions or degenerating bodies is asserted.

sections.heading: Why the result holds
paragraphs: At a constrained minimizer, the gradient points nonnegatively along every segment into the convex body. Taylor's formula therefore supplies the nonnegative quadratic upper proxy g. After scaling it to u=g/G, contraction toward the minimizer compares every sublevel volume with a smaller one: F(t)≤(t/s)ⁿF(s) for 0<s≤t, where F(t)=volₙ{x∈K:u(x)≤t}.

An explicit Dirichlet polynomial has a positive core of width proportional to the inverse square of its degree and a controlled tail. A fixed even power makes it a global square. Every dyadic tail shell is bounded relative to the same core mass that lower-bounds the normalizing integral. That mass cancels before summation, leaving the quadratic rate. The degree calculation and a constant-density fallback cover every positive integer order.

For K=[0,1] and f(t)=t, the note also proves the classical lower estimate Hᵣ(f,K)≥1/[4(r+1)²]. The same estimate holds for f(t,y)=t on [0,1]×[−1,1]^(n−1). Together with the upper theorem, this gives a fixed worst-case instance of order r⁻² in each dimension. It does not give a positive matching lower rate for every objective; constant objectives have zero error.

sections.heading: Scope and limitations
paragraphs: The note addresses the convex-body/Lebesgue regime in Laurent's contribution, joint work with de Klerk, to the 2018 Oberwolfach report. It explicitly uses probability densities of unit mass. Slot and Laurent's Theorem 11 gives the earlier O((log r)²/r²) bound for this hierarchy and asks whether the logarithm can be removed.

The constrained-gradient and quadratic-upper-estimator reductions already appear in de Klerk–Laurent and Slot–Laurent. Endpoint polynomial localization and comparison of shell mass with local core mass have classical precedents, including Totik–Varga. Their older endpoint-polynomial theorem, combined with Markov's inequality and the relative-mass argument, also yields the scoped quadratic upper rate. The interval/product worst-case exponent is likewise prior work of de Klerk–Laurent. No firstness or new-method claim is made, and present worldwide open status is not certified.

The theorem uses Lebesgue measure and a quadratic proxy. It does not assert the same rate for arbitrary reference measures or for the restricted hierarchy whose densities must be polynomials of the original objective for general nonconvex f. The construction assumes a global minimizer is available; it does not supply an efficient way to locate one or compute all required integrals. The explicit constant is coarse, rather than an optimal asymptotic coefficient.

The complete source and verification archive accompanies the paper. Finite exact checks and numerical examples supplement the written universal proof; they are not certificates of its infinite quantifiers.

A seven-hyperplane counterexample to a generic-initial degree bound

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript and declared publication date 15 October 2026 · No version declared · Unrefereed preprint

Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Original abstract

For the characteristic-zero arrangement defined by Q=xy(x-y)(x-2y)zw(x+z+w), the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal of the ambient Jacobian ideal has pure-second-variable cutoff 8 and a degree-7 minimal generator whose largest variable is the third. This explicitly contradicts the second-variable bound of Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli, also stated in OWR Report 5/2021. We prove the generic sectional dimensions on a nonempty open set of compatible flags, using scalar polar syzygies and Hilbert–Burch, and give exact rational checks. The arrangement is a classical parallel connection; the methods and the valid three-variable arrangement theorem are prior work. Historical novelty and independent discovery are not established. This unrefereed note was developed with extensive AI assistance and has not undergone conventional human peer review.

The idea in plain English

A generic initial ideal records the monomial structure of polynomial equations after a general linear change of coordinates. This note gives a seven-hyperplane arrangement whose Jacobian ideal violates a proposed bound linking a second-variable exponent to the degrees of generators involving the third variable.

The precise result

Let K be any field of characteristic zero, S=K[x,y,z,w], and Q=xy(x−y)(x−2y)zw(x+z+w). Form the ambient Jacobian ideal J=(∂Q/∂x,∂Q/∂y,∂Q/∂z,∂Q/∂w) using all four partial derivatives before taking any section.

For the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal B with variable order x₁>x₂>x₃>x₄, the pure-second-variable cutoff is p=min{d≥0:x₂ᵈ∈B}=8. The full four-variable ideal B has a degree-seven minimal generator in K[x₁,x₂,x₃] divisible by x₃. Its largest variable is therefore x₃, and its degree is strictly below p.

This contradicts the general-dimensional second-variable bound in Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli's Conjecture 5.7 and the matching Oberwolfach statement. In the former notation, the proposed threshold is d₀+1=p. The theorem holds over every characteristic-zero field, without assuming the field is algebraically closed.

Why the result holds

The proof studies compatible binary and ternary linear sections while keeping all four ambient polars. Reducing a linear polar relation modulo each distinct factor turns it into scalar proportionality equations with a trace condition. On the stated open conditions, there are no ternary linear syzygies and exactly one binary linear syzygy.

The binary polars have no common projective zero, so the ideal has height two. The classical Hilbert–Burch theorem forces syzygy coefficient degrees 1,2,3. The resulting Hilbert values are H₂(6,7,8)=(3,1,0) and H₃(5,6,7)=(21,24,24).

An explicit compatible flag shows that the required conditions hold on a nonempty open set. Intersecting that set with the generic-initial open set justifies the generic sectional values. Favorable ranks in one coordinate system alone would not establish this step.

Strong stability and the reverse-lexicographic section identity give the cutoff eight. Multiplication by x₃ in the first-three-variable quotient has kernel dimensions zero at degree six and one at degree seven. A minimal-divisor argument then gives the degree-seven generator and proves its minimality in the full ring: a divisor of a monomial in the first three variables cannot introduce x₄.

Scope and limitations

The ternary section retains four ambient partial derivatives. It differs from the three-generated Jacobian ideal obtained by restricting the arrangement and then differentiating in three variables. The valid three-variable theorem of Marchesi–Palezzato–Torielli remains intact.

The arrangement is a classical parallel connection of U_(2,4) and U_(3,4) along the shared factor x, as in Falk–Proudfoot. The logarithmic derivation mechanism, Hilbert–Burch theorem, Galligo generic-initial theory, Conca section identity and sectional counting methods are prior work. Tohaneanu explicitly credits Orlik–Terao for the derivation mechanism.

Migliore–Nagel's applicable family theorem already gives the resolution 0→S(−7)³⊕S(−9)→S(−6)⁵→J^(top)→0, where J^(top) is the intersection of the codimension-two primary components of J. This is substantive prior information about the family. That five-generated ideal differs from the four-generated ambient Jacobian ideal studied here.

The full text of Ilardi's 2018 article was unavailable for the priority comparison, so a relevant earlier theorem or family is not excluded. Historical parameter families and code were not exhausted. Firstness, independent discovery, a new arrangement or general method, and present worldwide open status are not established.

The result does not compute the full generic initial ideal, specify an exponent vector for the degree-seven generator, prove a positive-characteristic extension, or claim the smallest possible number of hyperplanes. Exact checks at specified rational coordinates supplement the open-set proof; they are not full-generic-initial or priority certificates.

A seven-hyperplane counterexample to a generic-initial degree bound

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript and declared publication date 15 October 2026 · No version declared · Unrefereed preprint

Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Complete source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record · CC BY 4.0

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Original abstract

For the characteristic-zero arrangement defined by Q=xy(x-y)(x-2y)zw(x+z+w), the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal of the ambient Jacobian ideal has pure-second-variable cutoff 8 and a degree-7 minimal generator whose largest variable is the third. This explicitly contradicts the second-variable bound of Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli, also stated in OWR Report 5/2021. We prove the generic sectional dimensions on a nonempty open set of compatible flags, using scalar polar syzygies and Hilbert–Burch, and give exact rational checks. The arrangement is a classical parallel connection; the methods and the valid three-variable arrangement theorem are prior work. Historical novelty and independent discovery are not established. This unrefereed note was developed with extensive AI assistance and has not undergone conventional human peer review.

The idea in plain English

A generic initial ideal records the monomial structure of polynomial equations after a general linear change of coordinates. This note gives a seven-hyperplane arrangement whose Jacobian ideal violates a proposed bound linking a second-variable exponent to the degrees of generators involving the third variable.

The precise result

Let K be any field of characteristic zero, S=K[x,y,z,w], and Q=xy(x−y)(x−2y)zw(x+z+w). Form the ambient Jacobian ideal J=(∂Q/∂x,∂Q/∂y,∂Q/∂z,∂Q/∂w) using all four partial derivatives before taking any section.

For the degree-reverse-lexicographic generic initial ideal B with variable order x₁>x₂>x₃>x₄, the pure-second-variable cutoff is p=min{d≥0:x₂ᵈ∈B}=8. The full four-variable ideal B has a degree-seven minimal generator in K[x₁,x₂,x₃] divisible by x₃. Its largest variable is therefore x₃, and its degree is strictly below p.

This contradicts the general-dimensional second-variable bound in Bigatti–Palezzato–Torielli's Conjecture 5.7 and the matching Oberwolfach statement. In the former notation, the proposed threshold is d₀+1=p. The theorem holds over every characteristic-zero field, without assuming the field is algebraically closed.

Why the result holds

The proof studies compatible binary and ternary linear sections while keeping all four ambient polars. Reducing a linear polar relation modulo each distinct factor turns it into scalar proportionality equations with a trace condition. On the stated open conditions, there are no ternary linear syzygies and exactly one binary linear syzygy.

The binary polars have no common projective zero, so the ideal has height two. The classical Hilbert–Burch theorem forces syzygy coefficient degrees 1,2,3. The resulting Hilbert values are H₂(6,7,8)=(3,1,0) and H₃(5,6,7)=(21,24,24).

An explicit compatible flag shows that the required conditions hold on a nonempty open set. Intersecting that set with the generic-initial open set justifies the generic sectional values. Favorable ranks in one coordinate system alone would not establish this step.

Strong stability and the reverse-lexicographic section identity give the cutoff eight. Multiplication by x₃ in the first-three-variable quotient has kernel dimensions zero at degree six and one at degree seven. A minimal-divisor argument then gives the degree-seven generator and proves its minimality in the full ring: a divisor of a monomial in the first three variables cannot introduce x₄.

Scope and limitations

The ternary section retains four ambient partial derivatives. It differs from the three-generated Jacobian ideal obtained by restricting the arrangement and then differentiating in three variables. The valid three-variable theorem of Marchesi–Palezzato–Torielli remains intact.

The arrangement is a classical parallel connection of U_(2,4) and U_(3,4) along the shared factor x, as in Falk–Proudfoot. The logarithmic derivation mechanism, Hilbert–Burch theorem, Galligo generic-initial theory, Conca section identity and sectional counting methods are prior work. Tohaneanu explicitly credits Orlik–Terao for the derivation mechanism.

Migliore–Nagel's applicable family theorem already gives the resolution 0→S(−7)³⊕S(−9)→S(−6)⁵→J^(top)→0, where J^(top) is the intersection of the codimension-two primary components of J. This is substantive prior information about the family. That five-generated ideal differs from the four-generated ambient Jacobian ideal studied here.

The full text of Ilardi's 2018 article was unavailable for the priority comparison, so a relevant earlier theorem or family is not excluded. Historical parameter families and code were not exhausted. Firstness, independent discovery, a new arrangement or general method, and present worldwide open status are not established.

The result does not compute the full generic initial ideal, specify an exponent vector for the degree-seven generator, prove a positive-characteristic extension, or claim the smallest possible number of hyperplanes. Exact checks at specified rational coordinates supplement the open-set proof; they are not full-generic-initial or priority certificates.
